mioc-078.title: The Andes cast a rain shadow over Patagonia
mioc-078.text: Mountains can make deserts. As the southern Andes rose 14 to 12 million years ago, their rain shadow created the Patagonian Desert to the east. A rain shadow forms when orographic uplift makes weather systems drop their precipitation on one side of a range, leaving little moisture for the other. Dating of metamorphosed layers suggests the Magallanes Basin and the Andean fold-thrust belt were exhumed between 10 and 4 million years ago.

mioc-089.title: The Paratethys turns brackish and its sea life dies
mioc-089.text: The sea did not simply return; it changed character. After open-marine conditions from 13.36 to 12.65 Ma, the Bârlad Strait reopened and the Central Paratethys turned brackish. This change caused the Badenian–Sarmatian extinction event. Meanwhile the Eastern Paratethys moved the other way: when the strait reopened, its lake levels dropped as it became a sea again.

mioc-095.title: The Eridanos, a lost river, builds a giant delta
mioc-095.text: A river from Lapland once built a delta to rival the Amazon's. By about 12 Ma, a minimum age, the Eridanos, flowing from Lapland across the Baltic region, had reached the North Sea area. Its sediments built an immense delta, reckoned comparable in size to the modern Amazon's. Remnants turn up from the North Sea and the Netherlands in the west to northern Lapland. Neogene uplift of the South Swedish Dome later deflected the river from its path across south-central Sweden to a course south of Sweden in the Pliocene.

mioc-099.title: The Amazon runs across a continent
mioc-099.text: The Amazon once flowed the wrong way. In the Cretaceous the proto-Amazon ran west, part of a river system draining from Africa. Between 11.8 and 11.3 Ma it began flowing as a river across the whole continent. The result is the largest river in the world by discharge, and the second-longest or longest river system, a title disputed with the Nile. Its average discharge of about 215,000 to 230,000 cubic meters per second is greater than the next seven largest independent rivers combined.

mioc-102.title: Europe's big mammals decline
mioc-102.text: Europe lost many of its big animals in the Late Miocene. Large mammal diversity fell significantly. The cause lay in a slow change of climate: over the Miocene it cooled gradually towards a series of ice ages. In Iberia, as the climate dried, grazers diversified while browsers declined.

mioc-111.title: The modern Yangtze takes shape
mioc-111.text: The Yangtze, the longest river of China and the third-longest in the world, is younger than its size suggests. The modern river is estimated to have originated around 11 Ma, and sedimentation rates suggest its present outlet is no older than the late Miocene. It rises at Jari Hill in the Tanggula Mountains of the Tibetan Plateau and flows 6,300 kilometers east to the East China Sea.

mioc-120.title: Ten-million-year-old apes of East Africa
mioc-120.text: Ten million years ago, apes close to our own family tree lived in East Africa. Ten-million-year-old hominid apes, Chororapithecus from Ethiopia's Afar rift and Nakalipithecus, are known from there. The gorilla branch split from the human–chimpanzee branch around then, at 10 Ma. The Rift Valley, an active continental rift zone, has been a rich source of hominid fossils for studying human evolution.

mioc-124.title: The Rivera microplate breaks away
mioc-124.text: Off western Mexico, a piece of the seafloor came loose. Around 10 Ma the Rivera plate broke away from the Cocos plate and became a microplate. Some sources give 10 to 5 Ma for this split. The Cocos Plate is a remnant of the Farallon Plate. It is still being subducted, pushed under Central America, where it dives beneath the North America and Caribbean Plates.

mioc-126.title: Oreodonts fade as deer and bovids arrive
mioc-126.text: North America's mammals changed cast in the Hemphillian age, from about 9.4 Ma. The last oreodonts, mylagaulids and dromomerycids died out. In their place, deer, bovids, saber-toothed cats and skunks arrived from Asia, while rabbits and short-faced bears diversified. The Hemphillian North American Land Mammal Age spans 9–4.75 Ma, and the Blancan follows from 4.75–1.6 Ma. Sources differ on exactly where the Hemphillian starts.

mioc-133.title: The Lake Malawi basin begins to form
mioc-133.text: Lake Malawi is older than anyone once thought. Its basin began forming about 8.6 Ma, far earlier than believed, though deep water first appeared only 4.5 Ma. The Malawi rift belongs to a linear chain of rift lakes that extends from the southern tip of the Red Sea to Mozambique. Lake Malawi is the southernmost lake in that line.

mioc-142.title: The Banda Arc meets Australia
mioc-142.text: An island arc ran into a continent. In the Messinian, the Banda Arc began colliding with Australia and Timor. It is a standard example of an island arc colliding with a continent to build an orogen, a mountain belt. Such a collision has a side effect: the subduction zone switches to the other side of the island.

mioc-148.title: Thalassocnus, the sloth that swam
mioc-148.text: A ground sloth went to sea. The oldest fossils of Thalassocnus, a ground sloth adapted to marine life on South America's Pacific coast, date to roughly 7 Ma in Peru. It is now known from many Miocene–Pliocene units along that coast, including Chile's Coquimbo Formation. Ground sloths themselves evolved mainly in South America during the late Paleogene and Neogene, while the continent was isolated.

mioc-156.title: Ardipithecus appears in East Africa
mioc-156.text: The human line was already separate from the chimpanzee line when Ardipithecus appeared. Our ancestors split from the ancestors of chimpanzees around the end of the Miocene, during the final Messinian Stage (7.5–5.3 Ma). The genus appeared around 5.5 Ma, probably after the split, while gene flow may still have continued. An early form, A. kadabba, joined Sahelanthropus and Orrorin among the first hominins in Africa at the very end of the Miocene. Its Middle Awash fossils date 6.5–5.5 Ma, and one timeline places Orrorin and Ardipithecus at 6 Ma.

mioc-159.title: The Dead Sea Transform forms
mioc-159.text: Near the end of the Miocene, the map of the Middle East was redrawn. The Arabian plate began colliding with Eurasia, the Dead Sea Transform developed, and rifting in the Gulf of Suez ceased. The transform is the boundary between the Arabian and African plates, a left-lateral series of faults between the Sinai Peninsula and the Arabia Plate. Left steps in it have opened a series of wrench basins, including the Dead Sea.

mioc-162.title: The Miocene ends in warmth
mioc-162.text: The Miocene ended on a warming note. Global temperatures rose again as the swing in Earth's axial tilt grew, increasing aridity in Central Asia. The Pliocene began warmer than the cool Messinian. The Miocene-Pliocene boundary also coincides with the time of the Messinian salinity crisis.

plio-003.title: The first tree sloths
plio-003.text: Sloths took to the trees around the start of the Pliocene. The first tree sloths appeared then. Early megalonychid sloths were small and perhaps partly tree-dwelling; by the Pliocene they reached about half the size of later Megalonyx. Living tree sloths are thought to have evolved from ground sloth ancestors, which makes ground sloths a paraphyletic group. During the Pliocene and Pleistocene, as part of the Great American Interchange, more sloth lineages migrated into Central and North America.

gela-009.title: Ethiopian waters join the Nile
gela-009.text: The Nile's flood owes its silt to Ethiopia. About 2.5 Ma waters from Ethiopia flowed north for the first time and joined the ancestral Egyptian Nile. Nile silt is eroded and carried only in the Ethiopian rainy season, when rainfall is especially high in the Highlands; the rest of the year the major rivers draining Ethiopia flow more weakly. Farther south, uplift of the Rwenzori Mountains turned paleolake Obweruka's drainage east and began forming Lake Victoria, which did not yet drain north.

gela-010.title: Lake Bungunnia dams the Murray
gela-010.text: Earth movements blocked the Murray River near Swan Reach and made a lake. Vast, freshwater Lake Bungunnia lasted from 2.5 to 0.5 Ma. The damming followed more than 250 m of uplift in the Grampians of Victoria about 2.5 Ma. When the lake drained, it appears to have marked the end of a wet phase in the Murray–Darling Basin and the onset of widespread arid conditions similar to today.

gela-015.title: The Amazon settles into its present course
gela-015.text: The Amazon had already been a transcontinental river since 11.8–11.3 Ma, as {{ref:mioc-099}} describes. It took its present shape about 2.4 million years ago. Geological studies suggest that for millions of years before that the river flowed in the opposite direction, from east to west. So the river that crosses the continent is old, but its present layout is young.

gela-017.title: Wind-blown dust builds the Loess Plateau
gela-017.text: A dusty wind-blown blanket began to build in northern China. Crustal movement and a cold climate started loess deposition on the Loess Plateau about 2.4 Ma. Tibetan uplift had set up the East Asian monsoon, and the drier Quaternary climate weathered out the silt that became loess. The Chinese Loess Plateau is one location where loess data has been very useful in understanding past climate.

gela-020.title: Giant ground sloths walk into North America
gela-020.text: Giant sloths walked north over a new land bridge. Eremotherium eomigrans, the first megatheriid ground sloth in North America, arrived 2.2 Ma across the new Panamanian land bridge. Eremotherium and Megatherium are the largest known ground sloths, thought to have had body masses of 3.5-4 tons. Traffic ran both ways in the Great American Interchange: horses that entered South America evolved into Hippidion around 2.5 Ma, and more ground sloth lineages migrated into Central and North America.

gela-027.title: The Congo basin takes its present shape
gela-027.text: Between about 2.0 and 1.5 Ma the basin of the Congo River acquired its present shape. The Congo Basin has a total area of about 4,000,000 km2, or 13% of the entire African landmass.

gela-048.title: The first Missoula floods scour the Scablands
gela-048.text: The Channeled Scablands were scoured long before the last ice age. The oldest Pleistocene Missoula floods swept through them sometime before 1.5 million years ago. The age rests on interglacial calcretes between flood deposits, magnetostratigraphy and luminescence dating. The floods blasted away the nurturing soils of the Palouse and much of the basalt beneath them.

gela-054.title: The Mesa Falls eruption at Yellowstone
gela-054.text: Yellowstone's second cycle peaked about 1.3 Ma in the Mesa Falls Tuff eruption, over 280 km³, forming Henry's Fork Caldera inside the Island Park Caldera. High-precision argon dating puts it at 1.3001 ± 0.0006 Ma. Over the past 2 Ma three very large explosive eruptions at Yellowstone have yielded approximately 900 cubic kilometers of felsic magma, about 900 times the volume of the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens.

gela-058.title: The Gregory Rift begins to pull apart
gela-058.text: Africa has been splitting for a long time, and still is. The Gregory Rift, the eastern branch of the East African Rift, began spreading about 1.2 Ma and still opens about 3 mm a year. Faulting then followed large shield-volcano eruptions near the craton's edge between 5 and 1 Ma. When rifting reached the Tanzanian Craton, the rift split into the eastern Gregory Rift and the western Albertine Rift, separated by the 1,300 kilometres wide East African Plateau. It results from the separation of the Somali plate from the Nubian plate, driven by a thermal plume.

gela-072.title: Straight-tusked Palaeoloxodon leaves Africa
gela-072.text: The largest elephant may have outweighed the largest land mammals of any age. At the end of the Early Pleistocene, about 800,000 years ago, the elephant genus Palaeoloxodon spread out of Africa and across Eurasia. One species, P. namadicus, is suggested to have had a body mass surpassing 16 tonnes, rivalling or exceeding paraceratheres, the otherwise largest known land mammals.

chib-002.title: The last chalicotheres, horses with claws
chib-002.text: The chalicotheres were odd browsers with claws instead of hooves. Their group, the Ancylopoda, ran from the Eocene into the Middle Pleistocene, and these last ones belong to its final stretch. They were herbivorous perissodactyl mammals, browsing with long, curved, cleft claws. Morphological evidence indicates they diverged from the tapirs, rhinoceroses and horses after the Brontotheria. One source lists chalicotheres among groups that went extinct in the Pliocene.

chib-009.title: Tiny ancestors of the Flores 'hobbit'
chib-009.text: Flores's small people had small ancestors. Teeth and a partial jaw from hominins thought ancestral to Homo floresiensis lived at Mata Menge about 700,000 years ago. They were as small as or smaller than the later Liang Bua remains, so the species' small size stayed stable for hundreds of thousands of years. The teeth are similar in size and shape to those of H. floresiensis but more primitive. These hominins likely arose from insular dwarfism acting on Homo erectus.

chib-010.title: A 'ghost' lineage splits from modern humans
chib-010.text: Modern humans carry DNA from a lineage no fossil has yet named. An archaic hominin population broke away from the modern human lineage around 700,000 years ago. Its DNA entered some sub-Saharan hunter-gatherer groups, such as the Biaka and San, about 35,000 years ago. West African groups such as the Yoruba and Mende carry it too, which shows it was acquired long before agriculture spread.

chib-015.title: The Rockland eruption at Lassen
chib-015.text: More than 130 km³ of rhyolite magma erupted violently from the Lassen area of California, with huge pyroclastic flows and an ash plume tens of kilometres high. Recent studies put the Rockland ash at up to 326.7 km³, over twice the Mazama ash, so the Rockland tephra could be the most voluminous eruption in the Cascade Volcanic Arc. From 600,000 to 400,000 years ago, eruptions then built the large conical stratovolcano Mount Tehama. Another source rounds the comparison with Mazama to nearly twice.

chib-016.title: The Great Barrier Reef builds its first full reefs
chib-016.text: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, made of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands. Its earliest evidence of complete reef structures dates to about 600,000 years ago, and coral skeleton deposits there go back about half a million years. Ribbon reefs and deltaic reefs form only in the northern part.

chib-025.title: The first brown bears
chib-025.text: Brown bears are recent arrivals in the bear family. Ursine bears originated around five million years ago, with extensive hybridization among the different species. The first brown bears appeared around 0.5 million years ago. The founding population of most North American brown bears arrived first, with its genetic lineage developing around 177,000 years ago.

chib-032.title: The mammoth steppe is born
chib-032.text:
During the MIS 12 glacial, about 460,000 years ago, a new kind of landscape appeared. The steppe-tundra biome, also called the mammoth steppe, first emerged, uniting animals of the northern tundra and Central Asian steppe. It would repeatedly expand and contract with later glacial cycles. At its peak it was once the Earth's most extensive biome.

It was cold and dry and relatively featureless, though climate, topography and geography varied considerably. Its fauna was dominated by reindeer, muskox, saiga antelope, steppe bison, horses, woolly rhinoceros and woolly mammoth.

chib-037.title: The Clactonian tool industry
chib-037.text: Not every early toolmaker made handaxes. From about 0.4 Ma, Homo heidelbergensis developed its own tool industry, the Clactonian, dated to the early Hoxnian Interglacial, around 424-415,000 years ago. It differs from the contemporaneous Acheulean mainly in not using handaxes; thick irregular flakes struck from a flint core served as choppers. Its distinctiveness has been questioned, because its techniques resemble the Acheulean and handaxes occur in Britain both before and after it.

chib-038.title: The first modern grey wolves
chib-038.text: The earliest specimens of the modern grey wolf date to around 400,000 years ago, possibly as early as 1 million years ago. Between 400,000 and 300,000 years ago dholes and wolves were similar in size, but wolves were slowly growing larger. It is widely agreed that the lineage goes back 2 million years to Canis etruscus, followed in the Middle Pleistocene by Canis mosbachensis. A 2010 study found that Canis diversity fell by the end of the Early to Middle Pleistocene, leaving in Eurasia the small C. mosbachensis-C. variabilis wolves and the large hypercarnivorous Canis (Xenocyon) lycanoides.

chib-039.title: The first polar bears
chib-039.text: Polar bears are young, and their exact birthday is uncertain. The first appeared about 400,000 years ago. Estimates of when they split from brown bears differ: a 2010 study gave about 150,000 years ago and a 2012 study about 600,000 years ago. Glaciation events over hundreds of thousands of years led to their origin and to their later interactions and hybridizations with brown bears.

chib-059.title: The last mesotheriids of South America
chib-059.text: A burrowing, rodent-like giant of South America made its last stand. Mesotherium, the last mesotheriid and last of the Typotheria, has its final records around 220,000 years ago. It was a long-lived, superficially rodent-like notoungulate, the largest typothere, possibly weighing up to 100 kg. Afterwards Toxodontidae was the only notoungulate family to survive into the Late Pleistocene.

chib-066.title: Karymsky blankets Kamchatka in ash
chib-066.text: Karymsky, an active stratovolcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia, has been linked to a VEI 6 or larger eruption that spread ash over more than 1.5 million km².
